evidence.claim: The road’s names preserve different connections: F.T. Valley Road takes its initials from Francis Thornton, whose name also belongs to Thornton Gap.
evidence.quote: F.T. stands for Francis Thornton, whose name was also applied to Thornton Gap west of Sperryville.

evidence.claim: Sperryville became a junction for several turnpikes in the 1850s, linking it with Culpeper, New Market and the Rappahannock River.
evidence.quote: In the 1850s several turnpikes were constructed that accessed Sperryville: Thornton’s Gap from Culpeper to Sperryville, Newmarket & Sperryville, and Sperryville-Rappahannock from Sperryville east to the Rappahannock River.

evidence.claim: Later, the opening of Skyline Drive brought gasoline stations, lunch rooms and motels to the village.
evidence.quote: until the opening of Skyline Drive in the late 1930s. The area became saturated with gasoline stations, roadside businesses, lunch rooms, restaurants, and motels.

evidence.claim: At the southern end of this drive, Madison retains the old US 29 alignment on Main Street, while the main highway now passes southeast of town. Route 231 continues to share that older street.
evidence.quote: Through the entirety of their trip through the town, both highways follow Main Street. US 29 Bus is the old alignment of U.S. Route 29, which now bypasses the town just to the southeast.

evidence.claim: Travel south from the US 522 junction southeast of Sperryville, passing Ashbys Corner and crossing the upper Hazel River toward Peola Mills and the Hughes River.
evidence.quote: SR 231 passes through Peola Mills as the highway enters Rappahannock County just north of its crossing of the Hughes River. The state highway crosses the upper reaches of the Hazel River and passes through Ashbys Corner before reaching its northern terminus at a wye junction with US 522 (Sperryville Pike) southeast of Sperryville.

evidence.quote: It consists of a village with two main streets along the two branches of the Thornton River, together with surrounding pasture and farmland.

evidence.claim: Manufacturing later added another layer of housing. The historic district includes homes built for Smoot tannery workers from 1867 into the early twentieth century, alongside wood-frame residences later converted to businesses.
evidence.quote: The buildings are predominantly wood-frame, one-and two-story residences, some of which have been converted to commercial establishments. They include a collection of former factory workers' housing built to serve the workers of the Smoot tannery from 1867 to the early 20th century.

evidence.claim: The village’s apple industry followed: an apple-processing facility opened in 1918, and a packing and juice plant later occupied the former tannery site.
evidence.quote: An apple processing facility was built in 1918 to serve the many local apple orchardists.

evidence.quote: The Sperryville apple packing and juice plant was created on the site of the former Smoot tannery.

evidence.claim: Old Rag’s exposed rocky summit distinguishes it from most mountains in the Blue Ridge.
evidence.quote: In contrast to most mountains of the Blue Ridge, Old Rag has an exposed (rocky) summit.

evidence.claim: The rock beneath the mountain is Old Rag Granite, formed during the Grenville mountain-building event about a billion years ago.
evidence.quote: Old Rag Mountain is underlain by Old Rag Granite, named for its ubiquitous exposure on the mountain, formed during the Grenville Orogeny about a billion years ago.

evidence.claim: The summit is in Shenandoah National Park, and the approach from Nethers branches from Route 231.
evidence.quote: the peak is located within Shenandoah National Park

evidence.claim: The summit is in Shenandoah National Park, and the approach from Nethers branches from Route 231.
evidence.quote: The shorter, most common way is from a parking area in Nethers near the end of Madison County's SR 601, off Virginia State Route 231, at the base of the mountain.

evidence.claim: On the Ridge Trail, the ascent reaches a false summit before becoming a rock scramble for 1.1 miles to the top, a section that can be strenuous for inexperienced hikers.
evidence.quote: The circuit hike makes use of the Ridge Trail which ascends the mountain 1.6 miles (2.6 km) to the first false summit. The trail then turns into a rock scramble, which can be strenuous for inexperienced hikers, for 1.1 miles (1.8 km) to the summit

evidence.claim: The Saddle Trail descends past two shelters to Weakley Hollow Fire Road, which forms the return leg of the circuit.
evidence.quote: the Saddle Trail which descends 1.9 miles (3.1 km) down the saddle of the ridge past Byrds Nest #1 shelter and Old Rag shelter to the junction with Weakley Hollow Fire Road. The Fire Road then descends 2.5 miles (4.0 km) to the Old Rag parking area.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service announced day-use tickets for each Old Rag hiker March 1–November 30 in 2022, in addition to the park pass fee.
evidence.quote: In 2022, the National Park Service announced the requirement of day-use tickets for each hiker between March 1 and November 30.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service announced day-use tickets for each Old Rag hiker March 1–November 30 in 2022, in addition to the park pass fee.
evidence.quote: The day-use ticket is in addition to the Shenandoah National Park pass fee.

evidence.claim: Main Street carries both Route 231 and the old alignment of US 29 through Madison; the main US 29 route now bypasses the town to the southeast.
evidence.quote: Through the entirety of their trip through the town, both highways follow Main Street. US 29 Bus is the old alignment of U.S. Route 29, which now bypasses the town just to the southeast.

evidence.claim: The county courthouse, built in 1828, is a two-story brick building with an open arcade across its front and a tall, domed octagonal cupola.
evidence.quote: It was built in 1828, and is a two-story,  brick temple-form structure.  On the facade the ground floor becomes an open arcade four-bays wide and one-bay deep.  The gable roof is topped by a tall octagonal domed cupola.

evidence.claim: It anchors a historic district of houses, commercial buildings and institutions dating from the early nineteenth through the twentieth century.
evidence.quote: In addition to the separately listed Madison County Courthouse, there are a variety of residential, commercial, and institutional buildings dating from the early 19th to the 20th century.

evidence.claim: The county clerk’s office dates to 1832, and the district also includes the Arcade from the 1830s, among the district’s nineteenth-century civic and commercial buildings.
evidence.quote: Notable buildings include the County Clerk's Office (1832), the Washington Tavern or Eagle House (ca. 1832), the Arcade (1830s)

flags: Cache gives present road names and connections, but no construction history for Route 231 or agency explanation of its scenic merits. Regional turnpike history is distinguished from the numbered highway; no claim those turnpikes are identical to Route 231.

Current claim that the designated byway begins at Gordonsville is unsupported: the cached byway list lacks its table, and the route article only says almost all SR 231 is a byway. The mapped northern portion is described without assigning legal designation boundaries.

Old Rag’s permit note records the 2022 National Park Service announcement in the cache, not confirmation of the 2026 rule. Required checked date is the batch’s cache-review date. A current park-manager source is needed before publication; no fees, availability or parking instructions invented.
